title: Browser feed cleansing and element removal
what: Judge each item as it loads and hide what does not earn the space.

shape.state: the text of one feed item
shape.question: a single noul question, asked hundreds of times
shape.answer: a probability per item; your code hides or keeps

use: A content script walks the loaded items, asks one narrow question of each, and collapses the ones that fail. The video's example hides posts that read as machine-generated filler; the same shape hides ads or cookie notices. Because one call answers in a fraction of a second, the page still feels instant if you judge only the items actually in view.

code.label: one question per post, in the page

title: Semantic in page search
what: Find the paragraph you meant, not the words you typed.

shape.state: the query, plus the candidate sections
shape.question: choice over the sections, by key
shape.answer: the section to scroll to, or no match

use: Split the document into sections, name each one, and ask which matches the query in meaning. Because the answer is a typed key rather than a sentence, the interface can scroll straight to the element it names. It is fast enough to run while the visitor is still typing, which is what makes it feel like a native find.

code.label: query in, section out, scroll

title: Image and asset retrieval via metadata
what: Search a media library by what is in the picture, not by file name.

shape.state: the search term, plus the asset records
shape.question: choice over asset keys
shape.answer: the asset to open, or no match

use: File names are a poor index, so every asset gets text first: the prompt it was generated from, or a caption written by a cheap multimodal model at indexing time. Searching then becomes one typed decision over those records. The video's own note is that captions are nearly free at this scale, and the index is worth more than the model that wrote it.

code.label: caption once, decide on every search
